key_findings: 82.2% of CUS ratings were 4-5 (clinically acceptable); 83% of DISCERN scores ≥20/25
No significant CUS difference across ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok (p=0.157)
At least one platform missed reference diagnosis in 9/15 vignettes; all missed porphyria
Gemini had longest responses; Grok most linguistically complex
Single-query assessment — not stable accuracy estimates

title: Quality and Readability of Four AI Chatbots Answering Search-Derived Patient Questions About Primary Aldosteronism: A Cross-Sectional Comparative Study

abstract: Four AI chatbot configurations (GPT-5.5 via ChatGPT Plus, Copilot Smart mode, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Perplexity) evaluated on 17 primary aldosteronism questions using DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmarks, and GQS. Copilot had highest DISCERN (43.00) and EQIP (75.00). JAMA scores were 0 for ChatGPT/Gemini, 1 for Copilot/Perplexity. No readability met sixth-grade benchmark. Source transparency remained low.
key_findings: Significant differences in DISCERN (p<0.001), EQIP (p<0.001), JAMA (p<0.001), GQS (p=0.020)
Copilot highest DISCERN (43.00) and EQIP (75.00); Perplexity second (42.00/70.00)
JAMA scores: 0 for ChatGPT/Gemini, 1 for Copilot/Perplexity (source transparency low)
No readability measure met sixth-grade benchmark
Score differences do not establish factual accuracy or clinical superiority

key_findings: Compares 5 clinical decision support tools for the same periprocedural anticoagulation scenario

Proposes common output standard to improve cross-tool comparability and clinical utility

authors: Anqi Li, Zhixuan Ge, Yixuan Duan, Jiarong Qian, Chi-Yu Chen, MingYu Lu, Huan-Yu Hsu, Yu Gu, Yue Guo, Sheng Wang, Wei Qiu, Hanwen Xu

14 general-purpose frontier and medical LLMs evaluated
Supervised finetuning and RL improve performance, suggesting real-world discussion trajectories support model adaptation
Three M.D. expert reviewers confirmed high information coverage and factuality

authors: McBain RK, Huang E, Figueroa C, Zhang LA, Cantor J

Published in BMJ Mental Health

title: Prospective multicentre expert evaluation of OneRx.AI oncology CDS in India
authors: Shekhawat M, Nagar AK, Gupta AA, Koshy AR, Sai Sankalp Naidu V, Kiran PK, Sathyakkagari N

Gwet's AC1 inter-rater reliability = 0.707
Exploratory ceiling-affected evaluation — Stage II study recommended

title: Counterfactual Auditing of Bias in Open-Source Large Language Models for Clinical Triage
authors: Manar Aljohani, Brandon Ho, Kenneth McKinley, Dennis Ren, Xuan Wang
abstract: Comparative counterfactual audit of ten open-source LLMs for pediatric Emergency Severity Index (ESI) prediction. Constructs paired counterfactual variants changing demographic, socioeconomic, healthcare-access, behavioral, social, or system-context variables while holding clinical presentation fixed. Models include Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, QLoRA fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B, MedGemma variants, MedLLaMA2-7B, GPT-OSS-20B, and GPT-OSS-120B. Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B showed lowest sensitivity (5.27% any-shift rate) vs 16.02% for base model. Larger or medical-domain models showed more significant shifts. Supports counterfactual auditing as lightweight, clinically interpretable framework for comparing fairness risks in open-source LLMs before clinical deployment.
relevance: Counterfactual bias audit of open-source LLMs for clinical triage — directly evaluates fairness risks in clinical decision support deployment
key_findings: Counterfactual sensitivity varied substantially and did not consistently decrease with larger model size or medical-domain pretraining
Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B showed lowest overall sensitivity: 5.27% any-shift rate vs 16.02% for base model
Several larger or medical-domain models showed more significant counterfactual shifts
Stratified analyses revealed clinically important directionality and shared failure patterns hidden by aggregate rates
scale: 10 open-source LLMs, pediatric ESI counterfactual vignettes

title: MedKIT: Evaluating Knowledge Integration and Generalization in Large Language Models
authors: Lukas Thede, Yash Kumar Atri, David Chen, Danielle Bitterman, Matthias Bethge, Tom Hartvigsen, Zeynep Akata
abstract: MedKIT (Medical Knowledge Integration and Transfer) benchmark providing granular evaluation of how models integrate and apply knowledge under realistic sequences of clinical updates. Each instance corresponds to a factual update derived from clinical evidence, paired with targeted probes assessing transfer across lexical variation, relational transformations, compositional reasoning, and open-ended operationalization, plus locality tests for knowledge preservation. Large-scale empirical study of 12 knowledge integration strategies across 5 diverse models. Results reveal consistent gap between recall and usable knowledge: most methods achieve strong gains on original update task and lexical variation, but relational generalization is limited, and no method yields meaningful improvements on compositional or operational tasks.
journal: arXiv preprint (cs.CL) — Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Datasets Track
relevance: Medical LLM benchmark evaluating knowledge integration under realistic clinical evidence updates — directly assesses whether models can use updated knowledge safely
key_findings: Consistent gap between recall and usable knowledge across all methods
Strong gains on original update task and lexical variation, but relational generalization limited
No method yields meaningful improvements on compositional or operational tasks
Highlights fundamental challenge in knowledge integration for medical LLMs

title: Prediction Is Not Detection: Evaluating Pre-Recognition Claims in Longitudinal Clinical AI
authors: Jing Yang, Long R. Jiao, Xiujun Cai, Zongjiu Zhang
abstract: Clinically useful early detection requires validated pre-recognition lead time. Event-based evaluations of longitudinal clinical AI can treat recognition-mediated care-process signals as shortcuts and recognition-dependent endpoints as reference standards, inflating apparent performance and lead time while undermining cross-center transport. Defines an interval-censored pre-recognition transition, an independent as-of reference standard, and a prespecified recognition proxy to make the claim testable.
relevance: Evaluation framework for longitudinal clinical AI pre-recognition claims — directly addresses validity of clinical AI performance measurement
key_findings: Event-based evaluations can inflate apparent performance and lead time by treating recognition-mediated signals as shortcuts
Defines interval-censored pre-recognition transition as independent reference standard
Proposes prespecified recognition proxy to make pre-recognition claims testable

title: SHIFT-M3: Pre-fusion Alignment-based Consistency Screening for Multimodal ECG Record Integrity
authors: Md Ashik Khan, Md Nahid Siddique
abstract: Studies multimodal record integrity triage for clinical AI: given an assembled record, should its modalities be trusted to belong together? SHIFT-M3 is a lightweight text-based pre-fusion screen measuring alignment between LLM-generated ECG interpretations and clinical report summaries. On 784,680 MEETI ECG records achieves 97.6% TPR@5% FPR for full text-view swaps (AUROC 0.996), 90.3% for partial swaps (AUROC 0.974). Introduces CMST evaluation taxonomy, three-seed stability study, loss ablation, temporal-tolerance sweep, and shared-token masking control. Accepted at MLHC 2026.
relevance: Multimodal clinical AI safety — addresses cross-patient record linkage failures that standard predictive models cannot detect
key_findings: 97.6% TPR@5% FPR for full text-view swaps (AUROC 0.996)
90.3% TPR for partial swaps (AUROC 0.974)
97.7% TPR for label-matched hard negatives (AUROC 0.996) with only 573K parameters
Main failure mode: longitudinal ambiguity — 87% Type-II false positives for same-patient cross-visit pairs

title: Periodontitis Risk Assessment and Prevention Planning: Comparative Study of Multimodal Large Language Models and Periodontist Evaluations
authors: Swinckels L, Alves Rabelo K, Delamare EL, Loos BG, Lahoud P, Bijwaard H, de Keijzer A, Kim J, Bruers J
abstract: Vignette study evaluating M-LLMs for periodontitis risk assessment from EHR data and panoramic radiographs. Three LLMs compared to periodontist. GPT o1 Pro (86.7%) and Claude Sonnet 4 (85.6%) showed strong performance comparable to periodontist (87.8%); Gemini 2.5 Pro significantly lower (59.4%). Radiographic interpretation consistently received lowest scores. GPT took 3min22s vs Claude 10s vs periodontist 5min57s.
relevance: Multi-LLM clinical comparison against specialist for periodontal risk assessment — directly benchmarks clinical AI tools
key_findings: GPT o1 Pro 86.7% and Claude Sonnet 4 85.6% acceptable ratings vs periodontist 87.8%
Gemini 2.5 Pro significantly lower at 59.4% (P<.002)
Radiographic interpretation consistently lowest scores across all models
GPT took 3min22s, Claude 10s, periodontist 5min57s
scale: 10 periodontal vignettes with panoramic radiographs and EHR data

authors: Széll A, Yu Y, Oeding JF, et al.

title: Clinical Concept Centers in LLMs
authors: Nagar A, Vaidyanathan A, Kaliya-Perumal AK, Boey ETH, Winkler S

summary: Extends behavioral evaluation of clinical LLMs into latent space, finding dedicated clinical concept centers in all 11 open-weight models tested. Concept centers are interpretable, causally drive model behavior, and predict clinician preferences in blinded validation. Introduces latent-space evaluation methodology for clinical AI.

Concept centers causally drive model behavior in constrained and open-ended settings
Models maintain coherence under adversarial priming; aligned priming improves performance
Steering along concept centers yields downstream clinical improvements
Blinded clinician validation: concept center activation predicts clinician preferences

Key extraction fields: specimen type 0.995, location 0.981, diagnosis 0.981
Hybrid LLM extraction + guideline-encoded rules approach
Would improve guideline adherence by reducing undersurveillance

title: LLM-Generated Electronic Consultations: Blinded Comparison of OpenEvidence vs Gastroenterologist eConsultations
scale: Mayo Clinic health system, blinded comparison
key_findings: Blinded comparison of OpenEvidence-generated vs gastroenterologist-written electronic consultations. Evaluates clinical quality, accuracy, and safety.

title: OpenEvidence clinical question-answering platform: systematic review of early evaluations
key_findings: First systematic review of OpenEvidence. 11 studies included. OpenEvidence generated clinically relevant, evidence-supported responses with lower fabricated citation rates than general-purpose LLMs.

title: Evaluator-Masked Assessment of 4 Consumer-Facing Large Language Models on Expert Anterior Segment Ophthalmology Questions
scale: 45 expert questions x 4 LLMs x 5 metrics x 11 evaluators (9900 ratings)
key_findings: Claude and Grok rated more favorably than ChatGPT and Gemini on quality metrics (Friedman P<0.001). No significant difference in mean safety scores, but Claude (35.6%) and Grok (33.3%) had more severe safety rating tails vs ChatGPT (6.7%) and Gemini (11.1%).

title: Evaluating different large language model performances in evidence-based dental implantology
scale: 16 clinical questions x 4 LLMs x 3 specialist evaluators
key_findings: LLaMA 3.2 + RAG significantly outperformed all other models (p<0.001) with median scores: Specificity 9.0, Accuracy 9.5, Clinical Utility 10.0. RAG access to structured guidelines significantly enhanced response quality. Inter-rater reliability was slight (kappa 0.078-0.180).

title: Concordance between large language models and orthodontists in photo-based orthodontic assessment
scale: 104 patients x 2 LLMs x 3 expert orthodontist evaluators x 5 clinical questions
key_findings: Mean ratings generally >=3 (moderate clinical acceptability). ChatGPT-4o rated significantly higher for treatment approach in Dental Class I patients. LLMs may provide clinically acceptable outputs as supportive tools under professional supervision, but variability persists in complex decision-making tasks.

source: J Am Coll Emerg Physicians Open
title: Automated Calculation of the PECARN Intra-Abdominal Injury Rule from Unstructured ED Notes Using a Large Language Model
journal: J Am Coll Emerg Physicians Open
scale: 196 children with complete ED notes, 2 urban pediatric EDs
key_findings: LLM calculated binary PECARN risk scores with 95.4% accuracy, 94.4% sensitivity, 98.2% specificity, F1 0.97. Weighted Cohen's kappa 0.96. Predictor variable extraction >94% accuracy across all variables. LLMs comparable to clinicians for automated clinical prediction rule calculation.

title: ChatGPT (GPT-5.1) Differential Diagnosis in Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology
task: Differential diagnosis ranking in oral/maxillofacial pathology
key_findings: Top-1 accuracy 44.0% text-only, 43.3% text+image. Top-10 accuracy 80.7% and 82.9%. No significant image effect. Supports educational use, not clinical decision support.

title: LLM Chatbot Safety - Responses to Simulated Psychotic Ideation
task: Safety evaluation of chatbot responses to simulated psychotic ideation over 7 days
dataset: Simulated psychosis scenarios in 2 languages across 7 consecutive days
key_findings: ChatGPT became less affirmatory over time; DeepSeek stable; Replika more affirmatory. DeepSeek and Replika gave potentially harmful advice (antipsychotic discontinuation) in 21% and 37% of conversations. Need for explicit safety standards.

title: Medical Ethics Recommendations Across LLMs - Case-Based Audit
task: Medical ethics recommendation audit (binary yes/no on 60 ethics dilemmas)
dataset: 60 original medical ethics dilemmas across 4 domains, 3 runs each, temperature 0
key_findings: Yes rates: DeepSeek-R1 44.4%, Claude 42.4%, GPT-5 38.9%, Gemini 38.9%, Llama 16.7%. Significant model effect (P<.001). Fleiss kappa 0.55. Within-model stability 85-100%.

title: ChatGPT-3.5 vs ChatGPT-4.0 vs ERNIE Bot for COPD Care
key_findings: Comparative study of 3 LLMs on COPD care assistance performance.

title: LLM Chatbots for MRI Safety Conditions Retrieval (3-LLM Benchmark)
task: MRI safety condition retrieval for medical implants
dataset: 50 device configurations + 20 clinical pilot patients (1200 parameter-level outputs)
key_findings: ChatGPT-5.0 highest accuracy (0.94), Gemini 0.79, Claude 0.78. ChatGPT-5.6 pilot accuracy 0.98. All made errors requiring verification against manufacturer documentation.
relevance: LLM benchmark for medical safety information retrieval

title: Gemini-2.5-Pro vs GPT-5 for Lung Cancer MDT Decision Support
task: Lung cancer multidisciplinary team treatment recommendation
dataset: 150 consecutive lung cancer cases, 3 information levels, NL and JSON formats
key_findings: Gemini-2.5-Pro best F1 0.7603, accuracy 0.8647 at Level III NL. GPT-5 highest recall 0.9132 (JSON) but lower precision. LLMs promising as MDT adjuncts with clinician oversight.
relevance: LLM head-to-head in real-world MDT setting

title: CDSS vs Human Expert for Imatinib Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
task: Imatinib TDM error detection and dosing optimization
dataset: 60 virtual patients with deliberate data-quality errors (in silico)
key_findings: CDSS sensitivity 53% vs expert 45%, target attainment 55% vs 37% (P=.046). But 5 detrimental outcomes vs 1 for expert. Validates CDSS architecture for prospective trials.
relevance: CDSS vs human expert head-to-head in pharmacology

title: AI Delirium Risk Prediction vs 4AT Screening Tool (2002 Patients)
task: Delirium risk prediction in trauma ward patients
key_findings: AI predicted 87.3% of delirium cases vs 28.0% for 4AT. AI specificity 73.9% vs 96.3%. AUC 0.884. AI enables proactive risk management vs reactive screening.
relevance: AI vs validated clinical screening tool in prospective cohort

title: LLMs + CDS for Recurrent Pregnancy Loss Management (3-LLM Benchmark with CDS)
dataset: 25 clinical scenarios based on ESHRE 2018/2022 guidelines, with and without structured CDS
key_findings: Baseline compliance 44%/28%/20%. With CDS: 92%/84%/80%. All models significantly improved with CDS intervention. CDS+LLM combination creates reliable auxiliary tool for RPL management.
relevance: LLM benchmark with CDS augmentation for obstetrics

title: AI Chatbots for TPN Planning in Critically Ill Patients (4-Chatbot Benchmark)
task: Total parenteral nutrition planning for critically ill adults
dataset: 10 standardized clinical cases (30 TPN plans total)
key_findings: ChatGPT best (57.7% accuracy, 10/10 plans), Gemini 43.9% (6 plans), Perplexity 38.5% (4 plans), Copilot declined. All 30 plans had safety issues; 63.3% rejected. Common errors: electrolytes, micronutrients, monitoring. None suitable for independent use.
relevance: Multi-LLM safety benchmark for high-stakes clinical dosing

title: 3-LLM Ensemble for Clinical Guideline Harmonization (Penile Cancer)
task: Clinical guideline harmonization and Delphi-ready item generation
dataset: 5 penile cancer guidelines, 157 recommendations, 95 literature-derived items
key_findings: LLM ensemble extracted 157 recommendations, consolidated to 68 harmonized items. 15 uniformly supported, 53 divergent. Final output: 62 human-reviewed Delphi-ready items validated by 4 experts. Scalable, transparent approach.
relevance: LLM ensemble for clinical guideline synthesis

title: DPO-Aligned Llama-3-8B for ICD-10 Coding from Discharge Summaries
task: Automated ICD-10-AM and ACHI code assignment from discharge summaries
dataset: Mapped MIMIC-III subset + de-identified Australian hospital dataset
key_findings: DPO-aligned full-parameter model achieved micro-F1 0.7397 (MIMIC) and 0.7834 (Australian). DPO improved agreement with reference code sets vs SFT alone.
relevance: LLM fine-tuning for clinical coding accuracy

title: Decision language models as affordable and rapid alternatives to LLM judges of clinical generative AI
authors: Rotem Gershon, Seffi Cohen, Dean Ariel, et al.
tools_evaluated: Jev decision LM vs 12 LLM judges (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6, GPT-5.4)
scale: 118 pediatric answers, HealthBench binary criteria, MedHELM open-ended tasks, HealthBench Professional
key_findings: Jev Gwet AC2 0.50 matched or exceeded 7/12 LLM judges. On HealthBench Professional, matched GPT-5.4 on 91% of criteria. Frontier judges cost 73-294x more, 7-57x slower.

title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
authors: Andrew Zhang, Trinh T. L. Vuong, Sophia J. Wagner, et al.
tools_evaluated: Clinical System One (CS1) 4B vs open decision models up to 27B
scale: 12.4M Q&A from 3.6M patients, 963,408 held-out patients, 21 external datasets
key_findings: CS1-4B outperformed 27B on 13/14 tasks. 6.4x faster inference. Screening 17 clinical trial criteria placed 4x more eligible patients in top 20 vs keyword search, 690-fold fewer LLM tokens.

title: HIVMedQA: Benchmarking large language models for HIV medical decision support
authors: Cardenal-Antolin G, Fellay J, Jaha B, et al.
tools_evaluated: 7 general-purpose LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, etc.) + 3 medical LLMs (MedGemma-27B, etc.)
scale: Clinician-curated HIV-related open-ended Q&A (basic knowledge, clinical reasoning, patient vignettes, bias-modified scenarios)
key_findings: Gemini 2.5 Pro highest overall. Medical LLMs did not consistently outperform general-purpose. Several models sensitive to cognitive bias prompts. LLM-as-judge aligned better with clinician than lexical metrics.

title: Planner-Executor Style Multimodal Agentic System for Lung Cancer Screening CT Patient Questions
authors: Sakiyama K, Serapio A, Ye M, et al.
scale: 116 LCS CT reports, 699 simulated patient questions, 4-physician reader study on 100 responses
key_findings: Tool-calling accuracy 93.1%, self-regulation accuracy 92.6%. Clinical accuracy 78.9% perfect 5.0 scores (Gwet AC2=0.92). Patient understandability 73.2% perfect scores. Demonstrates safe multi-modal agentic AI for patient communication in LCS.

title: MedR-Bench Secondary Analysis: Case Mix and Protocol Constraints in Diagnostic LLM Conversations
authors: Li OM, Li SXT, Li Y
scale: 957 source case reports, 6,690 released runs, 5,719 first-feedback analyses
key_findings: Unavailable-information marker associated with +6.37pp fifth-response contact, but largely explained by case composition (within-report coefficient 1.05pp, NS). Case composition and protocol states should remain visible when evaluating diagnostic trajectories.

title: Quality-grounded component-wise evaluation framework for LLMs in TCM clinical decision support
authors: Wang H, Wang J, Wang Q
tools_evaluated: Proposed evaluation framework for TCM LLMs
scale: Conceptual framework proposing component-level precision/recall and error grading
key_findings: Proposes two pillars: authoritative knowledge structuring (guidelines, textbooks, Pharmacopoeia) and fine-grained component-wise evaluation. Decomposes TCM reasoning into minimal assessable units. Identifies critical errors causing medical harm as primary evaluation criterion. Aligned with WHO Traditional Medicine Strategy 2025-2034.

title: Robustness Gap of Large Language Models in Nephrology
authors: Soejima A, Kitano F, Ichikawa D, Shibagaki Y, Noda R
key_findings: Identifies robustness gap between LLM capabilities and clinical reliability requirements in nephrology. Highlights domain-specific challenges for LLM clinical deployment in kidney disease management.

title: RAG with GPT-4o for maxillofacial prosthodontics clinical questions
authors: Launardo V, Koseoglu M, Susanto L, et al.
scale: 15 high-complexity clinical questions, 5 maxillofacial prosthodontist expert panel, 5-parameter 5-point Likert evaluation
key_findings: No significant differences between GPT-4o and RAG-GPT-4o (all P>0.05). RAG provides verifiable factual grounding essential for clinical safety. Base LLM offers substantial clinical reasoning capabilities but RAG needed for accountability in specialized dental care.

title: LLM vs faculty rater scoring of medical student OSCE documentation
authors: Nash CJ, Pau CY, Chahin N, Gruppen LD, Kogan JR, Thé TS
tools_evaluated: GPT-4o mini (OpenAI API) vs faculty raters
scale: 433 medical student notes, 7 standardized OSCE cases, 30+4 iterations per note
key_findings: High internal consistency (ICC=0.94 numerical, 0.76 with rationale). LLM scores significantly lower than faculty (mean diff -1.12 on 1-4 scale, P<.001). Spearman r=0.43-0.53. Potential for automation with rubric refinement needed.

title: Clinical Reliability of LLM-Generated Information in Colorectal Care
key_findings: Evaluation of clinical reliability and accuracy of LLM-generated information for colorectal care decision support. Assesses safety of LLM outputs in colorectal surgery context.

title: Multilingual evaluation of GPT-4o-based primary care pre-visit chatbot
authors: Chen PL, Rao AA, Pugh S, Lu Y, Johnson KB
scale: 31 bilingual participants (11 Mandarin, 10 Spanish, 10 Hindi), 5 synthetic primary care cases, validated instruments (BUS-11, NASA-TLX, HCTS, TAM-PEU)
key_findings: English scored higher on usability (+0.15), conversation quality (+0.62), summary quality (+0.25, all P<.001). Gaps language-dependent: Spanish and Hindi declined, Mandarin showed neither (P=.087). Trust, workload, ease-of-use consistent. Addressable language-specific weaknesses rather than fixed limitation.

title: Numeric vs embedding pipelines for clinical risk prediction in ICU
authors: Ge A, Wu J, Wu X, et al.
tools_evaluated: XGBoost numeric model (458 features) vs XGBoost semantic model (LLM text embeddings)
key_findings: Numeric model better for 5/6 tasks (mortality AUROC 0.9010 vs 0.8351, P<.001). Embedding model better for 30-day readmission (0.6618 vs 0.5900, P<.001). False positives largely non-overlapping between pipelines, suggesting complementary value.

title: Ethical alignment of cardiovascular AI-DSS for coronary artery disease rule-out
authors: Drogt J, Jongsma K, Bluemink M, Haitjema S
scale: Qualitative study among prospective end users
key_findings: Qualitative study exploring ethical alignment of AI-DSS for CAD rule-out with clinical environment. Examines prospective end-user perspectives on integrating AI decision support into clinical workflows.

title: Medical Literature-Specific AI: OpenEvidence, Heidi Evidence, Consensus, and PubMed.ai in Lacrimal Drainage Disorders
key_findings: OpenEvidence: 90.9% correct, 0% incorrect. Heidi: 63.6% correct, 4.6% incorrect (2 hallucinations). Consensus: 54.5% correct, 4.6% incorrect. PubMed.ai: 31.8% correct, 22.7% incorrect, 9% no response. OpenEvidence had no factually incorrect responses.

title: Inaccuracy and Inconsistency of LLMs in Providing Precision Dosing Recommendations for Patients With Kidney Impairment
scale: 6 LLMs, 3 standardized vignettes, 6 investigators, cefepime and meropenem dosing
key_findings: Mean concordance with literature: 63% (range 28-94%). Inter-iteration variance up to 1000% in daily maintenance doses. OpenEvidence uniquely cited relevant sources universally; other LLMs confabulated citations. All recommended TDM but only Claude consistently acknowledged uncertainty.

title: MedCase-Bench: Temporally Held-Out Evaluation Suite for Clinical Case Report Generation
scale: MedCase-150K corpus, temporally held-out evaluation suite
key_findings: MedCaseAgent outperforms existing general-purpose and specialized medical LLMs and agents under both LLM-judged and rule-based evaluation. Blinded expert reviews confirm clinical relevance and evidence grounding.

title: Enhanced DUR CDS System Evaluation in Community Pharmacy (9000+ locations)
models_evaluated: Enhanced DUR CDS system (before vs after)
key_findings: Alert burden decreased 82.2% (142.0 to 25.3 alerts/100 Rxs). Pharmacist interventions increased 93.9% (5.2 to 10.0/100 Rxs). Improving alert relevance and actionability reduces cognitive burden while improving care.

title: LLM Clinical Benchmarking Evaluator-Dependent Divergence (JMIR AI)
description: 40 clinical vignettes x 6 criteria across 5 endovascular fields. 4 LLMs evaluated (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.3 70B). 2 LLM raters (Claude, GPT-4o). ICC(2,1)=0.153. AI raters use model-specific criterion interpretation patterns producing systematically different outcomes.

title: Automation Bias in LLM-Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning RCT (NEJM AI)
description: Single-blind RCT, 44 physicians, 264 diagnostic cases. ChatGPT-4o with error-free vs error-containing suggestions. Treatment group 14.0pp lower diagnostic accuracy (73.3% vs 84.9%). Top-choice accuracy 18.3pp difference (76.1% vs 90.5%). Automation bias persists despite AI literacy training.

title: Script Concordance Test LLM Clinical Reasoning Benchmark (NEJM AI)
description: 750 SCT questions from 10 international datasets. 10 LLMs vs 1070 medical students, 193 residents, 300 attendings. o3 highest (67.8%), GPT-4o (63.9%), o1-preview (58.2%), DeepSeek R1 (55.5%), Gemini 2.5 Pro (52.1%). LLMs matched students but not senior residents/attendings. Systematic overconfidence in reasoning-tuned models.

title: Comparative Cost of Care: 24 LLMs vs Physicians (NEJM AI)
description: 24 AI systems on 200 deidentified clinical notes. AI care cost 3.2x physicians ($314 vs $97/visit, P<0.001). 20 general-purpose systems ranged $209-599. 4 specialized medical systems 2.7x-3.5x. Cost-aware prompt reduced to 2.5x; parsimonious to 1.4x. AI recommended testing at 66% of visits where physicians ordered none.

title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Medical Coding Evaluation (NEJM AI)
description: 9 LLMs evaluated for ICD-10 coding on 500 ED visits. RAG system using >1M ED visits. RAG-enhanced GPT-4 favored for accuracy 447 vs 277 (P<0.001); specificity 509 vs 181 (P<0.001). Smaller open-access models also improved significantly with RAG.

title: NPC-RubricBench: Phase-Aware Benchmark for Longitudinal Cancer Care
description: 30 LLMs evaluated on 941 patient-phase units across 6 cancer care phases, 17,688 atomic criteria. Diagnostic performance does not carry over to downstream care. Decision errors dominated staging at 48.2%, decision omissions dominated work-up and follow-up at 33.4% and 30.4%.

title: MedJev: Zero-Shot System-One Medical Decision Making Benchmark
description: MedJev evaluated across 10 medical benchmarks. MedQA 72.5%, USMLE 75.4%, NEJM 80.1%. Patient-level AUROC 0.926 for in-hospital mortality. ECE 0.028-0.063, recalibration to 0.007 with 50-200 labeled examples.

title: LLM Thyroid Nodule Biopsy Decision Benchmark (J Clin Endocrinol Metab)
description: 7 LLMs (GPT-5, Claude 3.5/4.0/4.5, Llama 3.2-90B, Deepseek R1, OpenEvidence) and 94 clinicians on 100 thyroid nodule vignettes. LLM biopsy rates 46%-74%. LLM-clinician agreement moderate (alpha 0.372-0.453). Llama recommended biopsy in 8/8 cases where clinicians unanimously recommended against.

title: Five LLMs on Hip Arthroplasty Guideline Concordance (EKIT-Hip Benchmark)
description: 5 LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, Gemini Advanced, Consensus Premium) on 26 questions from German S3 guideline. GPT-4o highest accuracy 3.69/4, comprehensiveness 4.31/5. GPT-4o and GPT-4 good/excellent in 96.2% vs 57.7% for Consensus Premium. OR 51.8 for GPT-4o vs Consensus.

title: Five AI Chatbots Dental Emergency Management Multilingual Benchmark
description: 5 AI chatbots (ChatGPT-5.2, Gemini 3.1, DeepSeek-R1, Grok 4.20, Kimi K2.5) on 130 dental emergency questions, 3 languages, 27,300 responses. 92.96% correct overall. Gemini 3.1 highest (94.8%), ChatGPT-5.2 (93.5%), Kimi K2.5 (92.9%). MCQs highest accuracy (94.3%), WH questions lowest (91.5%).

title: GenAI Models Nasal Polyps Patient Questions Benchmark
description: Multiple generative AI platforms evaluated on accuracy, currency, relevance, understandability, and clinical safety answering common nasal polyp patient questions. Platforms differed significantly in all dimensions.

title: LLM Gait Classification Cerebral Palsy Benchmark (ChatGPT vs Gemini vs Claude)
description: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude on 15 cerebral palsy gait cases (5 Rodda patterns). Claude graph-based 73.3% accuracy (kappa=0.67), ChatGPT/Gemini 46.7%. Video-based 20-26.7%. Treatment recommendation agreement low across all.

title: ChatGPT Audiogram Interpretation Version Benchmark (4.0 vs 5.1)
description: ChatGPT-4.0 vs ChatGPT-5.1 on 100 audiograms (20 with masking errors). ChatGPT-5.1 significantly higher on 6/7 questions (P<.001). Effect sizes 0.53-0.94. Both struggled with flawed input data. Inter-rater kappa 0.74-0.78.

title: HerbWise Domain-Specific LLM Traditional Herbal Medicine Benchmark
description: HerbWise (ChatGLM3-6B) trained on 748,041 entries for traditional herbal medicine. Outperforms general-purpose and domain-specific models across THM tasks including knowledge QA, compound property prediction, and ADMET prediction. Uses RAG framework.
